learningObjective: Distinguish an event that was available by prediction time from a late-arriving event whose event timestamp alone makes it look eligible.
mediumRationale: A compact Mermaid flowchart makes one valid path and one forbidden path visibly cross a named prediction-time boundary. Deterministic SVG would add manual geometry without improving the topological lesson; semantic HTML is weaker at showing paths; interaction is unnecessary for a fixed cutoff; source-figure reuse adds licensing risk; and no visual leaves the distinction between event time and availability time abstract.

pages.insight: The data-inspection checklist emphasizes label noise, bias, and inspecting examples, but does not define temporal eligibility.
The experimentation checklist stresses trustworthy training and evaluation skeletons and full test-set evaluation.
The experimentation slide separates offline ground-truth metrics from online production metrics, motivating parity between historical data and serving conditions.
The production checklist explicitly asks about out-of-time test data, feature freshness, and target leakage.
The data-pipeline slide asks how often new data arrives and how raw data becomes model features.
The serving slide covers online updates, monitoring, and inference constraints but does not visualize historical availability.

agentReview.summary: Reviewed the complete article, relevant deck workflow pages, and authoritative feature-store and stream-time documentation. Recommended a compact flowchart with the prediction cutoff as the central boundary and a dashed path that reaches into not-yet-known data.

implementation.accessibility: The Mermaid source provides a complete accessible title and description. The cutoff, timestamps, valid path, and leakage path are directly labeled; solid and dashed paths plus node shapes preserve meaning without color; and the caption restates the inference.
